title: To Penshurst: occasion and genre
short: Jonson's praise of the Sidney family's Kent house (The Forest 2, 1616) is the founding English 'country-house poem'.
body: Penshurst Place, near Tonbridge in Kent, was the seat of Robert Sidney (1563-1626), younger brother of Sir Philip Sidney, created Viscount Lisle in 1605 and Earl of Leicester in 1618, and of his wife Barbara Gamage. Because Prince Henry (d. November 1612) appears as alive (ll. 76-77), the poem is usually dated c. 1611-12. It was printed as the second poem of The Forest in the 1616 folio. Addressing the house itself, Jonson adapts Martial's praise of working estates (esp. 3.58) and Horace's rural ideal to create a genre later imitated by Carew, Herrick and Marvell. G. R. Hibbard's classic essay defined the genre; Alastair Fowler later collected its examples.

title: envious show
short: Penshurst was not built to be envied for display, unlike the new 'prodigy houses' of Elizabethan and Jacobean grandees.
body: The poem opens by negation, defining Penshurst by what it lacks. 'Envious show' means display designed to excite envy (and perhaps display that itself envies rivals). Contemporary readers would think of huge new houses such as Theobalds, Burghley or Robert Cecil's Hatfield (built 1607-11), monuments of courtly ambition. Penshurst, a medieval house extended by the Sidneys, stands for continuity and use rather than conspicuous expense. The contrast returns in the last lines, where other lords' 'proud ambitious heaps' are opposed to Penshurst. Don Wayne reads the whole poem as a defence of a traditional ideal of community against new forms of wealth.

title: touch
short: 'Touch' is touchstone, a fine black stone (basalt or black marble) used for luxurious building and monuments.
body: Touchstone was originally the dark stone on which gold was tested by rubbing (OED, touch, n., sense of 'touchstone'), and by extension any costly black stone used in architecture and tombs. Along with marble, polished pillars and gilded roofs, it signifies imported, expensive splendour. The list echoes Horace, Odes 2.18.1-5 ('Non ebur neque aureum / mea renidet in domo lacunar'), where the poet's modest house has no ivory or gilded ceiling and no marble columns. Jonson transfers the Horatian topos of modest sufficiency from the poet to a great aristocratic house.

title: lantern
short: A 'lantern' is a glazed turret or cupola on a roof, lighting the interior; showy ones were famous enough that 'tales are told' of them.
body: In architecture a lantern is a structure on top of a dome or roof, with windows, admitting light (OED, lantern, n., architectural sense). Elizabethan and Jacobean prodigy houses were known for such features, and for grand staircases and courts, all of which Penshurst is said to lack. The line is read as a general jab at showy modern houses; no particular target is certain. 'Pile' in l. 5 simply means a large building, with no pejorative sense; 'ancient' stresses its age and lineage.

title: these grudg'd at
short: The line probably means that while those showy features are resented, Penshurst, without them, is revered all the same.
body: The syntax is compressed. The most common reading takes 'these' as the lantern, stairs and courts just listed: such things are grudged at (envied or resented), whereas Penshurst is reverenced 'the while' (all the while, meanwhile). An alternative takes 'these grudg'd at' as an absolute phrase meaning 'although these [splendours] are begrudged you', i.e. though you are denied them, you are revered. Either way the point is moral: respect follows not from display but from what the house is and does.

title: Dryads, Pan and Bacchus
short: Classical nature-deities populate the Kentish park: tree nymphs, Pan god of flocks, Bacchus god of wine, feasting under beech and chestnut.
body: The estate's 'mount' (a raised viewing mound in the park) is imagined as a sacred grove. Dryads are tree nymphs; Pan, the Arcadian god of shepherds; Bacchus, god of wine and revelry. The 'broad beech' recalls the opening of Virgil's first Eclogue ('patulae ... sub tegmine fagi'), signalling that Penshurst is a living Arcadia. This mythological colouring flatters the Sidneys, whose most famous member wrote the Arcadia, and makes the estate a place where classical pastoral and English country life meet. Raymond Williams later criticised exactly this kind of mythologising for hiding real rural labour.

title: the Sidney oak
short: An oak planted at Sir Philip Sidney's birth in 1554, still known as Sidney's oak, at whose 'great birth' the Muses gathered.
body: Philip Sidney (1554-86), poet, courtier and soldier, mortally wounded at Zutphen, was born at Penshurst on 30 November 1554, and an oak (the 'nut' is an acorn) was said to have been planted to mark it. The tree traditionally identified with it, Sidney's Oak, stood until it died in 2016, though its real age was probably far greater than the legend allows. 'Where all the Muses met' turns his birth into a mythic nativity attended by the goddesses of poetry, a compliment to the author of Astrophil and Stella, the Arcadia and the Defence of Poesy. The house is thus praised through its literary lineage, and Jonson, a poet, implicitly places himself in that line.

title: names cut in the bark
short: Woodland lovers ('sylvans') carve their names on the oak, inflamed with Sidney's love poetry: the classical lover's carving motif.
body: Carving a beloved's name on a tree is a commonplace of pastoral (Virgil, Eclogue 10.53-54; Ovid, Heroides 5.21-24; it recurs in As You Like It). Here the carvers are 'sylvans', forest beings or rustic folk, 'taken with his flames' - caught by the ardours of Sidney's love verse, or by the passion his memory inspires. 'Writhed' means twisted, describing the gnarled bark of an old oak. The two lines make the tree a living monument to Sidney's poetry.

title: satyrs, fauns and the lady's oak
short: Satyrs challenge fauns to race to 'thy lady's oak', a tree associated by tradition with a Sidney lady.
body: Satyrs and fauns are goat-legged woodland spirits of Greek and Roman myth, here sporting like country youths. 'Provoke' means challenge; 'lighter' means nimbler. 'Thy lady's oak' is by tradition 'My Lady's Oak', under which Barbara Gamage (Lady Sidney) was taken in labour; this is local tradition rather than documented fact. The point is that every feature of the park carries family memory, and the mythology is domestic and affectionate.

title: Gamage's copse
short: A copse (small wood) named after Barbara Gamage, Robert Sidney's Welsh heiress wife, which supplies venison in season.
body: Barbara Gamage (c. 1563-1621), of Coity Castle in Glamorgan, married Robert Sidney in September 1584; as a wealthy only child and heiress she had attracted many suitors, and the match was arranged largely for political and financial reasons, though it proved a happy one. Tradition says she liked to feed the deer in the shade of this copse. Naming the copse after her inscribes the lady into the landscape, preparing for her praise later in the poem (ll. 84-88, 90). 'Season'd deer' are deer killed in their proper season, ready for the table. Hunting and venison were aristocratic privileges, and 'exercise thy friends' refers to hunting as entertainment for guests.

anchor: Each bank doth yield thee conies
title: conies; Ashore and Sydney's copp's
short: 'Conies' are rabbits; Ashore (Ashour) and Sidney's copse are named woods on the estate, 'copp's' being coppices.
body: 'Coney' was the normal word for an adult rabbit (OED, coney, n.). The 'tops / Fertile of wood' are the wooded uplands of the estate, two of which Jonson names: Ashour wood and Sidney's copse, real places in the Penshurst park. 'Copp's' is a contraction of 'copses' (coppices: woods regularly cut for timber and underwood). The precise local names give the panegyric documentary weight, as if Jonson were walking the estate. Note the singular verb 'doth' with the plural subject 'tops', a common early modern licence.

title: willing game
short: Partridges, carp, pike and eels offer themselves to be eaten: a golden-age fantasy of nature's spontaneous generosity.
body: Birds 'lie' in every field and are 'willing to be kill'd'; fish 'pay thee tribute', pikes betray themselves 'officiously' (dutifully, eagerly), eels leap into the fisherman's hand. The motif comes from Martial 10.30, where the fish at Apollinaris' villa swim up to their master, and more widely from golden-age myth (Hesiod, Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.89-112), in which the earth gives without labour. Critics divide over its tone: some find gentle comic hyperbole, others (Raymond Williams, followed by many materialist readers) see a revealing ideological move by which the work and violence that supply the lord's table are made to vanish.

title: the Medway
short: The Kent river (actually its tributary the Eden runs by Penshurst) flows near the estate; if it fails, the fishponds supply the table.
body: The Medway rises in Sussex and flows through Kent to the Thames estuary; the Eden joins it near Penshurst. 'High-swoln' (swollen with flood) explains why the river might 'fail thy dish'. The estate's ponds then 'pay tribute', a political metaphor that makes the fish the house's loyal subjects. The house is imagined as a small kingdom whose produce comes to it as dues, an image that prepares for the king's visit later in the poem.

title: the orchard and the Hours
short: The orchard yields fruit in order, cherry to quince; 'new as are the hours' may personify the Horae, the classical goddesses of the seasons.
body: The fruits arrive 'each in his time', a picture of ordered abundance rather than sudden luxury; 'his' is the normal neuter possessive. The 'hours' may glance at the Horae, Greek goddesses of the seasons who preside over growth. The apricot and peach that 'Hang on thy walls, that every child may reach' are espaliered on walls, but the phrase also makes the abundance available to everyone, even children: the poem's ideal of generosity extending down the social order. Renaissance country-house poems commonly list fruits and game this way (compare Marvell's 'The Garden').

title: built with no man's ruin
short: Penshurst's walls were not built by dispossessing tenants or exploiting labour, so none of its neighbours wish it pulled down.
body: The line distinguishes Penshurst from houses raised on enclosure, rack-renting and eviction, which were contemporary grievances. 'Country stone' is local stone, not imported marble. 'Clown' (l. 48) means a peasant or rustic, without the modern comic sense (OED). Williams, in a famous critique, argues that the poem's moral contrast depends on erasing the labour that built and fed all such houses. Defenders reply that Jonson is setting an ideal standard against which actual landlords, including perhaps the Sidneys, could be measured. The debate has shaped later readings of the whole genre.

title: the tenants' gifts
short: Neighbours bring capons, cakes, nuts and cheeses without any suit to press, and send marriageable daughters bearing fruit: borrowed from Martial 3.58.
body: In Martial 3.58 the rustic visitor to Faustinus' farm does not come empty-handed ('nec venit inanis rusticus salutator'), bringing honeycomb, cheese and other farm produce, while the grown daughters of honest farmers offer their mothers' gifts in woven baskets. Jonson adapts this closely: 'no one empty-handed', 'ripe daughters', whose baskets of plums or pears are 'an emblem of themselves' (they are ripe for marriage, and the fruits carry erotic suggestion). 'Salute' means to greet formally; 'though they have no suit' means they ask no favour in return, stressing that the gifts are freely given love, not rent or bribery.

title: Martial and the working estate
short: The gifts add nothing needed to a house already abundant; the point, as in Martial 3.58, is the contrast between a real farm and a sterile showplace.
body: Martial 3.58, addressed to Bassus, contrasts Faustinus' productive villa at Baiae with merely ornamental country places (idle myrtles, a 'widowed' plane tree, clipped box) that yield nothing for the table. Jonson adapts this into the poem's central contrast between a house that produces and gives and houses that merely display. 'Free provisions' means generous, liberal supplies; 'liberal board' (l. 59) means a generous table. The rhetorical question makes the tenants' gifts purely expressive: they 'express their love' but cannot add anything to such plenty.

title: equal fare for guests
short: At Penshurst the guest eats the lord's own food and drinks his own wine, unlike the humiliating dinners where clients got inferior fare.
body: Jonson's speaker, a poet-guest, now enters the poem as 'mine'. Roman satire had attacked patrons who served guests worse food than themselves: Martial 3.60, addressed to Pontice, asks why, now that the dole of food (sportula) is no longer given, he is not served the same dinner as his host, and Juvenal's Satire 5 describes the client Trebius' humiliations at Virro's table. 'Allow'd to eat, / Without his fear' means he may eat without anxiety. 'Of thy lord's own meat' means from the same dishes. The social egalitarianism is real but limited; Wayne notes how carefully the poet places himself within the household order.

title: dine away; fain
short: 'Not fain' means not obliged; 'dine away' means go away hungry, or dine elsewhere, after sitting at a great man's table.
body: 'Fain' here means constrained, obliged (OED, fain, a., sense of being compelled). The phrase 'sit ... and yet dine away' is variously glossed: the lesser guest at a grand table is seated, yet does not really dine (he is given poorer food than his host), or is in effect sent away to dine elsewhere. Jonson had personal grievances on this score: in the Conversations recorded by Drummond (1619), seated at the lower end of Lord Salisbury's table, he complains that he does not dine with his host, since he gets none of his lord's own dishes. The parenthesis 'as some this day' points the satire at contemporary hosts.

anchor: Here no man tells my cups
title: tells
short: 'Tells' means counts: no servant keeps count of how much the guest drinks, or looks grudgingly at his appetite.
body: 'Tell' in the sense 'count' survives in 'bank teller' and 'all told' (OED, tell, v.). The waiter does not 'envy' (begrudge) the poet's gluttony, because he knows there is plenty left 'below', in the servants' hall, where the same food will reach him. Jonson, well known for his size and appetite, makes a self-mocking joke about his own 'gluttony'. The passage again shows how the house's plenty runs through every level of the household.

anchor: For fire, or lights, or livery
title: livery
short: 'Livery' here is the allowance of food and drink delivered to a guest's chamber for the night, not servants' uniform.
body: The older sense of livery is anything 'delivered', especially rations or provisions given to servants or guests (OED, livery, n., sense of allowance of provisions). The guest at Penshurst does not have to beg servants for fire, candles or a night's allowance: 'all is there'. The extravagant conclusion, 'As if thou then wert mine, or I reign'd here', makes the poet momentarily the lord of the house, a fantasy that anticipates the royal visit that follows: in this house every guest is treated as a king, and the king himself is entertained.

title: King James and Prince Henry
short: James I and his son Prince Henry, arriving late from hunting, found the house ready to receive them; the visit helps date the poem before November 1612.
body: James I (reigned 1603-25) was a passionate hunter, and his heir Henry, Prince of Wales (1594-1612), was the hope of the Protestant party with which the Sidneys were associated. 'This way' means near here; 'brave' means splendid. Henry's death on 6 November 1612 provides the usual terminus for the poem's date. The episode is the climax of the hospitality theme: Penshurst, which entertains every rustic and poet generously, proves equal to an unannounced royal visit.

title: Penates
short: The Penates were the Roman gods of the household and its store-cupboard; the blazing hearths look as if their desire to welcome the king had caught fire.
body: In Roman religion the Penates guarded the household and its provisions (penus, food store); with the Lares they were worshipped at the hearth, and Aeneas carries Troy's Penates to Italy in the Aeneid. Jonson's conceit gives the house a soul: the fires on every hearth are the household gods' own desires burning to entertain the king. 'Sudden chear' (l. 82) means improvised entertainment and food ('cheer' in the sense of fare); the parenthesis 'great, I will not say, but' modestly claims that the welcome was not lavish, only immediate.

title: huswifry
short: Housewifery, the management of a household; the lady had linen, plate and rooms ready though she was away.
body: 'Huswifry' (housewifery) is the skilled oversight of a great household (OED). Lady Sidney had arranged that her linen and silver plate were at hand and every room dressed even while she was 'far' (absent). The praise turns domestic competence into a noble virtue, as 'high' suggests. It also has a political edge: a well-governed household was a type of the well-governed state, and the lady's preparedness for a royal guest proves the house's order.

title: legitimate children
short: Lady Sidney is noble, fruitful and chaste, so her husband can be sure his children are his, a fortune 'rarely known' in this age.
body: The lines are a sharp satirical aside. Jacobean court culture was notorious for adultery scandals, and Roman satire offered precedents, as in Martial's and Juvenal's jokes about husbands and other men's children. Barbara Gamage bore Robert Sidney a large family. The stray closing apostrophe after 'own;' in the archive text is a transcription slip, not part of the poem. The praise of chastity also prepares the final picture of a pious household.

title: mysteries
short: The children learn religion and the 'mysteries' (skilled crafts, secret arts) of courtesy, soldiering and learning, from their parents' example.
body: 'Mystery' in the sense of a craft or trade (from medieval Latin misterium, ministerium) survives in 'mystery plays' (OED, mystery, n.2), though the word also keeps its religious sense. The Sidney children are taught to pray morning and evening with the whole household, an image of Protestant domestic piety, and they read virtue in their parents' 'noble parts' (qualities) as in a book. Manners, arms and arts are the three accomplishments of the Renaissance gentleman, embodied supremely by Philip Sidney.

title: built / dwells
short: The closing antithesis sums up the poem: other houses are merely constructed monuments of pride; Penshurst is lived in, a true home.
body: 'Proportion' means compare, measure against. The 'proud ambitious heaps' return to the prodigy houses of the opening, bringing the poem full circle. The final contrast between building and dwelling carries moral weight: to 'dwell' implies residence, hospitality, continuity and responsibility to the community, whereas 'built' implies only expense. The poem is written in heroic couplets, and the epigrammatic final line shows Jonson's Martial-trained skill at closure. Critics from Hibbard to Wayne take this line as the key to the country-house ideal.
